[Option 1] Reusing the application's components and functionality built for the front stage users would provide both a unified best practice user experience, and a decoupled frontend application that minimises the reliance upon and customisations required to the Dynamics CRM. 

### Positive Consequences

* SEPA creates & relies upon a reusable set of back stage components that can be used by other project's requiring a web interface.
* Least reliance / lock in to CRM vendor, both in terms of customisations but also in terms of the domain specific resources required.
* Best support for evolutionary design & architecture - changing the standalone frontend application would be less costly compared to changing the CRM interface.  Facilitates hypothesis driven development.

* The Dynamics UI would retain it's default labelling, which could sit out of the context of 'permitting'.
* Additional resources required to maintain the standalone frontend application.
* A custom backstage needs to be considered in the wider SEPA architectural perspective.

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### 1. Create a custom web application 

A custom web frontend application pushes/pulls data either directly via the service APIs in the case where the user pushes files to Azure Blob Storage, or via a server side API gateway (built as part of the application) which utilises the Dynamics & Azure blob storage and Active Directory APIs.

#### Positive
* Full control over styling, interactions and journey.
* A modular / component based frontend build can be reused across other web projects.
* Separates display logic from the data layer - all data is managed in the CRM then consumed and displayed using API endpoints.
* Custom build pipelines can be used to manage the deployment & testing directly from the code repository.
* Minimises the customisation of Dynamics, reduces vendor lock in.
* Minimal domain specific knowledge required to configure and maintain frontend code.
* Reuses the front stage components to build the majority of the application, most back stage specific logic is related to workflow.
* Consistent best practice (reuse of gov.uk patterns) user experience for front and back stage users.
* When taking into account the front stage interface, this would seem to require the least amount of up front work.

#### Negative
* Built from the ground up, requiring more up front development time and resource.
* Additional time & effort require to manage, update and deploy as the codebase is managed by SEPA.  
* If Dynamics is not customised / configured to match the SEPA processes, the Dynamics UI would show labels / context that do not match the web interface.

Microsoft Dynamics 365 Web Portals provide an 'out the box' customisable web interface for their Dynamics systems.  The
styling, page elements & functionality can be customised using the open source templating library 'Liquid' which was created by Shopify.

* Web forms and lists can be setup for any custom workflow.
* Login and registration can be integrated with Azure Active Directory & Azure Active Directory B2C
* Multiple website can be setup, potentially allowing SEPA to handle multiple license types.
* All infrastructure and code management is handled within the Dynamics portal.

#### Negative
* Out of the box, CRM forms are targeted for sales, marketing and support so additional work is required to repurpose and restyle whats available.
* Increases vendor lock in - frontend code is stored within the CRM system.
* Without in-depth experience of this solution, it is not initially clear how much Web portals can support a custom journey, and if so, how difficult it would be to build (what level of custom coding woudl be required?).
* Potentially requires more domain specific knowledge & resources in terms of Dynamics, Portals & Liquid templating language, to customise and maintain this solution.

#### Positive
* Dynamics UI reflects the processes of the CCP permit application.
* Reuse of existing Azure AD logins, no additional auth components required.
* All infrastructure and code management is handled within Dynamics.
* Depending on SEPA's level of Microsoft 365 product integration, the Dynamics UI could support a consistent 'Microsoft' admin experience (and depending on who speak to, that could be considered a positive or a negative).

* Out of the box, CRM forms are targeted for sales, marketing and support so additional work is required to relabel the CRM for a unified context.

## Decision Outcome

[Option 2] Using Azure B2C with an existing 'Sign up and sign in' policy leverages the best out of the box authentication.  Users register and login using an Azure hosted service, users are redirected back to the application where a valid OAuth JWToken identifies who is currently logged in.

A custom domains would be best option, but this seems to be unavailable at the time of writing.

### Positive Consequences

* Leverages best practice for auth now and in the future.

### Negative Consequences

* Additional policy customisations would be required to fully customise the flow of the registration and login process (see links).
* Standalone HTML/CSS files will be need to be managed and uploaded to / updated in the Azure Directory  

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### 1. Custom resource policy

Custom resource policies can be setup to allow a 'resource own password credentials' flow, whereby the login is handled entirely 
within the application without redirecting to Microsoft URLs & the username/password is forwarded to Azure AD B2C. 

[Configure the resource owner password credentials flow in Azure Active Directory B2C using a custom policy](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory-b2c/ropc-custom)

[Resource Owner Password Credentials grant flow in Azure AD](https://joonasw.net/view/ropc-grant-flow-in-azure-ad)

[Why the Resource Owner Password Credentials Grant Type is not Authentication nor Suitable for Modern Applications](https://www.scottbrady91.com/OAuth/Why-the-Resource-Owner-Password-Credentials-Grant-Type-is-not-Authentication-nor-Suitable-for-Modern-Applications)

#### Positive
* Consistent user journey is maintained - user see's no change in the URL
* Can support custom journey designed in the prototype
* No additional coding/styling required.

#### Negative
* This login does not work if the user:
    * Has MFA
    * Is a federated account
* Complex policies required to support login, password reset 
* Potentially less secure
* This flow is based on 'existing trust relationship' with the client, "take special care when enabling this grant type and only allow it when other flows are not viable"

### 2. 'Sign up and sign in' on b2clogin.com

Sign up & login are initialised within the application but the user is redirected to a separate Azure domain where authentication happens.
Once authenticated, the user is redirected back to the application with the relevant authentication information stored in their browser as an OAuth token.

#### Positive
* 'Out the box' policies maintained by Microsoft
* Security updates inherited from Microsoft
* Authentication is potentially available across multiple Azure tenants (i.e. applications)

#### Negative
* User is taken to a separate URL (negatively impacting trust?)
* Separate code would need to be applied to the Microsoft page to maintain consistent branding.
* Browser autofill wouldn't pick up any SEPA.org.uk domain logins  

### 3. 'Sign up and sign in' on custom domain

Similar journey to option 2 however the Azure domain can be customised so that a SEPA sub-domain (e.g. login.sepa.org.uk) can be pointed to the Azure tenant. This would create a more consistent user journey. 

[How can we improve Azure AD - customer-owned domains](https://feedback.azure.com/forums/169401-azure-active-directory/suggestions/15334317-customer-owned-domains)

#### Positive
* Consistent user journey is maintained - ui can be styled, user doesn't see any change in URL
* The sub-domain could be a central login point for all SEPA services requiring authentication.
* User's browser is able to apply user's stored SEPA login details whereas using a MS url this wouldn't be possible.  

#### Negative
* This option doesn't seem to be available to all users yet. 
* Separate code would need to be applied to the Microsoft page to maintain consistent branding.

## Context and Problem Statement

We're building websites and web applications that share a common design system with reusable components. How do we write CSS styles in a way that is performant and safe?

## Decision Drivers

- Should be performant, with code splitting, caching and minimal runtime overhead.
- Needs to have easy access to our design system constants. These should optimally be shared with JS logic.
- Should be type-safe to catch issues when refactoring.
- Reusable components should be closed, not accepting arbitrary styles/classes.
- We want a pattern for responsive props with atomic layout components.

## Considered Options

- [CSS Modules](https://github.com/css-modules/css-modules) with [SASS](https://sass-lang.com/)/[PostCSS](https://postcss.org/)
- [Styled Components](https://styled-components.com/)
- [Treat](https://seek-oss.github.io/treat/)
human_decision:
# CSS

- Status: accepted
- Deciders: devs
- Date: 2020-05-26

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: Treat, because it combines the best of both worlds from CSS-in-JS and CSS modules.

We'll create shared components that have responsive props, but are otherwise closed for modifications. Theme variables are defined in a shared library with TypeScript.

Example:

```typescript
// Good:
<Box padding"small" />
<Box padding={{xs: 'small', md: 'medium'}} />
<Input large />
<Text preset="heading3" as="p" />
```

```typescript
// Bad:
<Box className={customLayout} />
<Input style={{ height: 50, padding: 16 }} />
<Text className={styles.heading} />
```

### Positive Consequences

- Treat is statically extracted at build time, so it has minimal runtime.
- Styles load in parallel with JS, also when code splitting.
- Styles are written in TypeScript which gives us type safety when referring to shared variables, styles and helpers.
- Styles are in special files, separate from markup and components giving us clear separation with good visibility into the rendered markup.
- We can pull in responsive layout component patterns from Braid, which gives us a good base to lay out components and pages.

### Negative Consequences

- We are choosing a pretty new framework, so it may 1) have bugs or issues, 2) be an obstacle for new developers or 3) be discontinued.
- When we're generating responsive styles at build time we need to be mindful at how many variations we allow (eg media queries, columns, whitespace), since they can easily bloat our CSS with unused styles.

## Pros and Cons of other Options

### CSS Modules with SASS/PostCSS

- Good, because it builds on top of standard CSS syntax which everyone knows.
- Good, because it has no runtime.
- Good, because it is separate from markup.
- Bad, because it is messy to generate advanced styles in a CSS-based language.
- Bad, because it's not type safe.

### Styled Components

- Good, because it's the industry leader in CSS-in-JS.
- Good, because it allows rendering pages with no redundant styles.
- Good, because it has excellent developer experience, making it easy to implement dynamic styles based on theme/props.
- Bad, because it's runtime may significantly affect site performance.
- Bad, because it hides the markup which may cause accessibility issues.
cot_answer:
To determine the best option for writing CSS styles that are performant and safe, let's evaluate each of the considered options against the decision drivers:

1. **CSS Modules with SASS/PostCSS:**
   - **Performance:** CSS Modules are known for their performance benefits, as they scope styles locally by default, reducing the risk of style conflicts. SASS/PostCSS can further optimize CSS with features like nesting and autoprefixing.
   - **Design System Access:** CSS Modules do not inherently provide a way to share design system constants with JS logic, but this can be managed with additional tooling or conventions.
   - **Type Safety:** CSS Modules do not provide type safety out of the box, but TypeScript can be used alongside to catch some issues.
   - **Reusable Components:** CSS Modules support encapsulation of styles, but they do not inherently prevent arbitrary styles/classes from being applied.
   - **Responsive Props:** CSS Modules do not provide a built-in pattern for responsive props, but this can be achieved with additional CSS or JS logic.

2. **Styled Components:**
   - **Performance:** Styled Components can introduce some runtime overhead due to dynamic style generation, but they support server-side rendering and caching to mitigate this.
   - **Design System Access:** Styled Components allow easy access to design system constants, as styles are written in JavaScript and can directly use JS variables.
   - **Type Safety:** Styled Components can be used with TypeScript to provide type safety, especially with props.
   - **Reusable Components:** Styled Components encourage encapsulation and do not accept arbitrary styles/classes unless explicitly allowed.
   - **Responsive Props:** Styled Components support responsive props through props-based styling, making it easy to create atomic layout components.

3. **Treat:**
   - **Performance:** Treat is designed for performance, with features like code splitting and minimal runtime overhead.
   - **Design System Access:** Treat allows sharing of design system constants with JS logic, as styles are defined in JavaScript.
   - **Type Safety:** Treat can be used with TypeScript for type safety.
   - **Reusable Components:** Treat supports encapsulation of styles and does not allow arbitrary styles/classes.
   - **Responsive Props:** Treat does not have built-in support for responsive props, but this can be managed with additional logic.

**Conclusion:**
- **Styled Components** is the best option given the decision drivers. It provides easy access to design system constants, supports type safety with TypeScript, and allows for responsive props with atomic layout components. While it may introduce some runtime overhead, its benefits in terms of encapsulation and integration with JavaScript outweigh this concern. Additionally, its ability to handle server-side rendering and caching helps mitigate performance issues.

# Unified Naming Strategy for Files and Directories

- Status: accepted
- Deciders: devs
- Date: 2020-07-03

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: Name files after their default export. If that default export is a React Component, or a class, then the file name should be in PascalCase. Otherwise, the filename should be in camelCase. Basically, for naming files avoid using kebab-case and snake_case and make sure the name follows the default export of the file.

Naming directories should follow these guidelines: Only use kebab-case when naming NX apps and libraries, or folders containing apps and libraries, e.g. `island-ui` instead of `islandUi`: `import { Box } from '@island.is/island-ui/core'`

Use PascalCase for directories only containing React components:

```text
components/CtaButton/index.ts
import 'components/CtaButton'
```

or:

```text
components/CtaButton/CtaButton.tsx
import 'components/CtaButton/CtaButton'
```

rather than

```text
components/cta-button/CtaButton.tsx
```

In all other cases, use camelCase.

### Positive Consequences

- Easier to navigate the codebase
- File names are more readable, and developers know what to expect
- This approach is the most common practice, and something most JS and TS developers are familiar with.

### 1. OAuth 2.0 + OpenID Connect

- **Secure**: OAuth 2.0, when combined with OpenID Connect, provides a robust security framework. OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0, which enhances security by providing authentication capabilities.
  
- **Well defined and well reviewed standard**: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect are both well-established standards. They have been widely adopted and reviewed by the security community, ensuring a high level of trust and reliability.

## Considered Options

Branching strategies:

- [GitHub Flow](https://guides.github.com/introduction/flow/)

# Branching and release strategy

- Status: accepted
- Deciders: devs, devops
- Date: 2020-05-24

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "OneFlow" because it provides a single eternal branch with well structured releases.

We'll implement OneFlow with these details:

- Release branches are set up the Monday after each sprint. This is sometimes called release trains, where features line up for different release trains.
- Release and quality managers from each team are responsible for reviewing and approving releases.
- Releases apply to all apps in the monorepo.
- Releases are versioned like this: `{cycle}.{sprint}.{hotfix}`. So version 3.1.2 is the release after cycle 3, sprint 1 with two hot fixes applied.
- Feature branches are merged using "Squash and merge", so they can be easily reverted.
- There are two ways to build larger features.
  - If the feature is isolated and not likely to cause conflicts, they can stay on long-living feature branches until they are ready to be released.
  - If the feature touches many parts of the codebase, it can be useful to merge changes more often but hide the feature in production with feature flags.
- If a project needs to deploy updates outside of the sprint rhythm, they should use hotfix branches.

### Future strategy

With time, we expect to build up better testing capabilities which gives us more confidence in the health of our monorepo. Then we can move quicker, with a simpler GitHub Flow branching strategy and continuous delivery into production.

### Hosting environments

We'll set up continuous delivery to different hosting environments:

| Environment | Git source            | Databases/services | Features |
| ----------- | --------------------- | ------------------ | -------- |
| sandbox     | feature branch        | Test               | All      |
| dev         | main                  | Test               | All      |
| staging     | main                  | Prod               | All      |
| pre-prod    | release/hotfix branch | Prod               | Finished |
| prod        | latest release tag    | Prod               | Finished |

We'll probably start with dev, staging, pre-prod and prod environments, since feature branch deployments are more dynamic and difficult to manage.

## Pros and Cons of Branching Options

### Git Flow

- Good, when there needs to be multiple versions in production.
- Good, because it enforces an easy to comprehend naming convention for branches.
- Good, because it has good support in popular git tools.
- Bad, because the git history becomes unreadable.
- Bad, because the main/develop split is redundant.

### GitHub Flow

- Good, because it fits well with Continuous Delivery and Continuous Integration.
- Good, a simpler alternative to Git Flow.
- Good, when we need to maintain a single version in production.
- Bad, because production code can become unstable most easily.
- Bad, if we need release plans.

### One Flow

- Good, because it has a clean git history (with squash-and-merge).
- Good, because it has a structured release process without multiple long running branches.
- Good, because it has good parts from GitHub Flow (simple history with one branch + feature branches) and Git Flow (releases and hot fixes).
- Bad, because it makes continuous integration more difficult.

## Pros and Cons of Release Options

### Continuous Delivery

- Good, because it is simpler and leaner, allowing changes to be deployed quicker.
- Bad, because it can easily break something in production if our CI isn't good enough.

### Release trains

- Good, because it has more structured releases, which helps with planning and QA.
- Good, because it can be synchronised to organisational schedule.
- Good, because it gives us a process to verify and test each release.
- Bad, because it is fairly rigid and complicated to implement organisation-wide.

## Links

- [4 branching workflows for Git](https://medium.com/@patrickporto/4-branching-workflows-for-git-30d0aaee7bf)
- [Branching patterns - Martin Fowler](https://martinfowler.com/articles/branching-patterns.html)

### Branching Strategies

1. **Git Flow**
   - **Pros**: 
     - Provides a structured approach with dedicated branches for features, releases, and hotfixes.
     - Good for projects with scheduled releases.
   - **Cons**:
     - Can be complex and may slow down the process due to multiple branches.
     - Not ideal for continuous deployment as it involves more manual steps.

2. **GitHub Flow**
   - **Pros**:
     - Simple and straightforward with a single main branch and feature branches.
     - Supports continuous integration and deployment well.
   - **Cons**:
     - Less structured than Git Flow, which might be challenging for teams new to a shared monorepo.

3. **OneFlow**
   - **Pros**:
     - Combines the simplicity of GitHub Flow with the structured release process of Git Flow.
     - Supports both continuous delivery and scheduled releases.
   - **Cons**:
     - May require some initial learning and adaptation.

### Release Strategies

1. **Continuous Delivery**
   - **Pros**:
     - Ensures that every change is ready to be released, providing high confidence in releases.
     - Works well with agile environments and supports quick feedback loops.
   - **Cons**:
     - Requires a robust automated testing and deployment pipeline.

2. **Release Trains**
   - **Pros**:
     - Provides a predictable release schedule, which can help teams plan better.
     - Can be easier to manage in a monorepo with multiple teams.
   - **Cons**:
     - May delay the release of features that are ready, as they have to wait for the next train.

### Evaluation

- **Confidence in Releases**: Continuous delivery and OneFlow provide high confidence due to their focus on ensuring every change is ready for release.
- **Structured Releases**: Git Flow and Release Trains offer more structure, but OneFlow also provides a balance between structure and simplicity.
- **Simplicity and Clear Takt Time**: GitHub Flow and Continuous Delivery are simpler, but OneFlow offers a good balance with its structured yet straightforward approach.
- **Agile Environment**: Continuous Delivery and GitHub Flow align well with agile practices, but OneFlow also supports agile workflows effectively.

### Conclusion

Considering the decision drivers and the pros and cons of each option, the best combination seems to be **OneFlow** for branching strategy and **Continuous Delivery** for release strategy. This combination provides a balance of structure and simplicity, supports agile practices, and ensures high confidence in releases. It allows for continuous deployment to QA, which aligns well with the need for simplicity and clear takt time.

# What API Management Tool to Consider

- Status: accepted

Technical Story: Design of Api Gateway / API Portal

### Requirements

Since the API Gateway is intended for students and startups to gather open government data, the following requirements need to be fulfilled. The student / startup is defined as Consumer of service. The organization that deliver the service as open service is defined as Provider of service. The open service is hosted on organizations X-Road server. The API Gateway must provide functionality for

- Registration of services with rate limit
- Self-service portal
- API key for Consumer
- Rate limit for Consumer

#### Provider

- Register open service in API gateway.
- Set rate limit on open service in API gateway.

#### Consumer

- Register as service user.
- Register application intended to use API (Consideration).
- Get API key for that application or consumer.
- Register what API to use in the application.
- Ability to test the API from API console with application API key (Consideration).

#### Considerations

API Keys / Rate Limits Is it sufficient to have only One API key for each Consumer, or is it required to define different Consumer applications with different API key. If a typical Consumer has created application and has valid API key, it is likely that he will not bother to register new application and get new API key. He could reuse the already given one. Consumer could also use the ability to register another application and get new API key with fresh rate limits.

Consumer registration What will be used to validate / approve students or startups for access on services. Should it be registered by SSN or some unique id, or only by email, with ability to reregister with new email again and again.

### Functional ability for decision

Functional ability to consider when evaluating the tool. The following list was taken from [wikipedia page for API Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/API_management).

- Gateway: a server that acts as an API front-end, receives API requests, enforces throttling and security policies, passes requests to the back-end service and then passes the response back to the requester. A gateway often includes a transformation engine to orchestrate and modify the requests and responses on the fly. A gateway can also provide functionality such as collecting analytics data and providing caching. The gateway can provide functionality to support authentication, authorization, security, audit and regulatory compliance.
- Publishing tools: a collection of tools that API providers use to define APIs, for instance using the OpenAPI or RAML specifications, generate API documentation, manage access and usage policies for APIs, test and debug the execution of API, including security testing and automated generation of tests and test suites, deploy APIs into production, staging, and quality assurance environments, and coordinate the overall API lifecycle.
- Developer portal/API store: community site, typically branded by an API provider, that can encapsulate for API users in a single convenient source information and functionality including documentation, tutorials, sample code, software development kits, an interactive API console and sandbox to trial APIs, the ability to subscribe to the APIs and manage subscription keys such as OAuth2 Client ID and Client Secret, and obtain support from the API provider and user and community.
- Reporting and analytics: functionality to monitor API usage and load (overall hits, completed transactions, number of data objects returned, amount of compute time and other internal resources consumed, volume of data transferred). This can include real-time monitoring of the API with alerts being raised directly or via a higher-level network management system, for instance, if the load on an API has become too great, as well as functionality to analyze historical data, such as transaction logs, to detect usage trends. Functionality can also be provided to create synthetic transactions that can be used to test the performance and behavior of API endpoints. The information gathered by the reporting and analytics functionality can be used by the API provider to optimize the API offering within an organization's overall continuous improvement process and for defining software Service-Level Agreements for APIs.
- Monetization: functionality to support charging for access to commercial APIs. This functionality can include support for setting up pricing rules, based on usage, load and functionality, issuing invoices and collecting payments including multiple types of credit card payments.

We recommend using hosted solution from **AWS** for API gateway. To determine the best option for exchanging information between the application menu and the window manager, let's evaluate each of the considered options based on the decision drivers: fast updates and no message loss.

1. **Shared Memory**:
   - **Pros**: Fastest method for inter-process communication (IPC) as it allows direct access to the same memory space.
   - **Cons**: Requires synchronization mechanisms (like semaphores) to manage concurrent access, which can add complexity. Also, it doesn't inherently handle message loss or ordering.

2. **Shared Files**:
   - **Pros**: Simple to implement and understand.
   - **Cons**: Slower due to file I/O operations. There's a risk of data corruption if not properly managed, and it doesn't inherently prevent message loss.

3. **Named Pipes**:
   - **Pros**: Provides a unidirectional or bidirectional communication channel. Easier to use than shared memory for simple message passing.
   - **Cons**: Can be slower than shared memory. There's a risk of message loss if the buffer is full and not read in time.

4. **Sockets**:
   - **Pros**: Very flexible and can be used for communication over a network or locally. Reliable if using TCP, as it ensures message delivery and order.
   - **Cons**: More overhead compared to shared memory, but still relatively fast for local communication.

5. **Message Queues**:
   - **Pros**: Designed for message passing, ensuring messages are not lost and are processed in order. Can handle complex communication patterns.
   - **Cons**: Slightly more overhead than shared memory, but generally efficient for IPC.

**Step-by-Step Evaluation**:
- **Speed**: Shared memory is the fastest, but message queues and sockets (especially with TCP) are also efficient for local communication.
- **Message Reliability**: Message queues and sockets (with TCP) ensure no message loss and maintain order, which is crucial for the application menu's requirements.
- **Complexity**: Shared memory requires additional synchronization mechanisms, while message queues and sockets provide built-in mechanisms for message handling.

**Final Decision**:
Considering the need for fast updates and no message loss, **Message Queues** are the best option. They provide a balance of speed, reliability, and ease of use for ensuring that the application menu receives updates about window states without losing any messages.

To select the best option for handling concurrency in the Volley Management system, let's evaluate the two considered options: Optimistic Concurrency and Pessimistic Concurrency, based on the decision drivers provided.

### Optimistic Concurrency

1. **Performance**: 
   - Optimistic concurrency control generally allows for higher throughput because it doesn't lock resources. Instead, it checks for conflicts only when a transaction is about to commit. This means that multiple transactions can proceed in parallel without waiting for locks, which is beneficial for performance in high-throughput scenarios.
   
2. **Maintainability**:
   - Implementing optimistic concurrency typically requires less code than pessimistic concurrency. It often involves adding version numbers or timestamps to records and checking these before committing changes. This approach is usually simpler and less intrusive than managing locks.

### Pessimistic Concurrency

1. **Performance**:
   - Pessimistic concurrency involves locking resources when a transaction starts, which can lead to reduced throughput. Transactions may have to wait for locks to be released, which can become a bottleneck, especially in high-throughput environments.
   
2. **Maintainability**:
   - Managing locks can add complexity to the codebase. It requires careful handling to avoid deadlocks and ensure that locks are released appropriately, which can increase the amount of code and the potential for bugs.

### Conclusion

Given the decision drivers of performance and maintainability, optimistic concurrency is the better option for the Volley Management system. It supports high throughput by allowing concurrent transactions without locking resources and requires less code to implement, making it easier to maintain. 

Therefore, the best option is **Optimistic Concurrency**.
comparison_result: 204 - Yes // Both decisions favor Optimistic Concurrency due to its performance benefits and alignment with Azure Table Storage.

Persistence and retrieval of SKOS taxonomies require a storage layer that supports storing rich, free-form linked data.
Such a data model could be represented in a traditional RDBMS, however, doing so would require a specialized serialization and deserialization implementation whereas graph databases can typically store RDF natively.

## Decision Drivers <!-- optional -->

* High availability/Fault tolerance
* Learning curve
* Maintenance overhead
* Vendor lock-in

## Considered Options

* Apache TinkerPop
* Apache Jena Fuseki
* PostgreSQL

# Selection of Graph Database software for SKOS taxonomy management

* Status: accepted
* Deciders: [@garyttierney](https://github.com/garyttierney), [@danielgrant](https://github.com/danielgrant), [@robmarch2](https://github.com/robmarch2)
* Date: 2019-05-23

Technical Story: DTM-34

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: Apache Jena with underlying PostgreSQL persistence store and a custom persistence layer, because it provides a highly available database persistence that is widely available as a managed service. We opted against using Apache Jena's SDB to achieve this as it has been in a state of "maintenance only" since June 2013.

### Positive Consequences

* PostgreSQL can be clustered, making it highly available
* PostgreSQL is broadly available as a managed service
* We can utilise the same PostgreSQL database for storing additional data (e.g. users, roles, etc)

### Negative Consequences

* We have to design our own schema and code for interacting with the PostgreSQL database

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Apache TinkerPop

TinkerPop is less of a graph database implementation and more of an abstraction layer over various graph database backends.
It presents a frontend consisting of a query language named "Gremlin", that uses a method chaining style of syntax to build graph queries.

Some of the backends TinkerPop supports are listed below:

* Azure CosmosDB
* Amazon Neptune
* Neo4J

#### Query example (TinkerPop: Gremlin)

```gremlin
g.V().has('id', 'http://example.com/skos-concept').out('skos:broaderConcept').values('skos:preferredLabel')
```

#### Persistence example (TinkerPop: Gremlin)

```gremlin
g.addV('skos:concept').property('id', 'http://example.com/skos-concept').property('skos:preferredLabel', 'value')
```

[Query language reference documentation](http://tinkerpop.apache.org/docs/current/reference)

* Good, because it supports various graph database backends.
* Good, because it relies on a standardized query language, making the persistence implementation almost graph database agnostic.
* Bad, because the query language is not designed for simple CRUD operations, and instead for determining relationships across graph edges.
* Bad, because it's an extremely heavyweight generalized solution for data fitting a very specific model.
* Bad, because there is an extremely high learning curve associated with the Gremlin query language compared to something like SPARQL or SQL.
* Bad, because it's built for Groovy first and the JVM second.

### Apache Jena Fuseki

Fuseki is a hosted backend for the Apache Jena SPARQL engine.
It allows storage of RDF data by first serializing it to turtles and querying it back using the Jena API, or by executing SPARQL queries.

#### Query example (Jena: SPARQL)

```sparql
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core/>
SELECT ?broader
{
  <http://example.com/skos-concept> skos:broaderConcept ?broader
}
```

#### Persistence example (Jena: API)

```java
RDFConnectionFactory connection = /* ... */;
connection.load("<http://example.com/skos-concept> <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#broaderConcept> <http://example.com/skos-broader-concept>");
```

* Good, because it can store SKOS in its native representation (RDF)
* Good, because it has an extensive Java API available.
* Good, because the query and persistence options are intuitive and easy to use.
* Bad, because it is the only maintained open source SPARQL server available.
* Bad, because it is self-hosted and would require maintenance (as well as deployment of a new unfamiliar technology).

### 1. Apache TinkerPop
- **Graph Database**: Apache TinkerPop is a graph computing framework that can work with various graph databases. It supports property graphs but does not natively support RDF, which is the format for SKOS taxonomies.
- **High Availability/Fault Tolerance**: This depends on the underlying graph database used with TinkerPop. Some databases like JanusGraph (which can be used with TinkerPop) offer high availability.
- **Learning Curve**: TinkerPop has a moderate learning curve, especially if the team is not familiar with graph computing concepts.
- **Maintenance Overhead**: Maintenance can be complex due to the need to manage both TinkerPop and the underlying graph database.
- **Vendor Lock-in**: TinkerPop itself is open-source and can work with multiple databases, reducing vendor lock-in.

### 2. Apache Jena Fuseki
- **Graph Database**: Apache Jena Fuseki is a SPARQL server that supports RDF natively, making it well-suited for SKOS taxonomies.
- **High Availability/Fault Tolerance**: Jena Fuseki can be configured for high availability, but it may require additional setup and management.
- **Learning Curve**: The learning curve is moderate, especially if the team is not familiar with RDF and SPARQL.
- **Maintenance Overhead**: Maintenance is relatively straightforward, but it requires knowledge of RDF and SPARQL.
- **Vendor Lock-in**: Jena Fuseki is open-source, reducing concerns about vendor lock-in.

### 3. PostgreSQL
- **RDBMS**: PostgreSQL is a traditional relational database that does not natively support RDF. Storing SKOS taxonomies would require custom serialization and deserialization.
- **High Availability/Fault Tolerance**: PostgreSQL offers robust high availability and fault tolerance features.
- **Learning Curve**: The learning curve is low if the team is already familiar with relational databases.

- **Vendor Lock-in**: PostgreSQL is open-source, so there is no vendor lock-in.

### Conclusion
Given the need to store RDF natively and the decision drivers, Apache Jena Fuseki is the best option. It directly supports RDF, which aligns with the requirement for storing SKOS taxonomies. While it has a moderate learning curve and requires some setup for high availability, it avoids the complexity of custom serialization/deserialization needed with PostgreSQL and the potential maintenance overhead of using TinkerPop with an additional graph database. Additionally, being open-source, it minimizes vendor lock-in concerns.

As a user, I want to get Changes metrics related to tasks defined
in a task tracker. A simple usecase example is to get insight of the
ratio of changes related to Feature Requests vs Bug fixing.

## Decision Drivers

* Simple implementation
* No assumption about the tasks tracker
* Support of a set of generic fields related to a task

## Considered Options

* Monocle API provides an interface for external task data crawlers
* Monocle provides crawlers for most popular task trackers
human_decision:
# 9. Changes extended with task data

* Status: accepted
* Deciders: Fabien Boucher
* Date: 2021-04-20

Technical Story: https://github.com/change-metrics/monocle/issues/301

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Monocle API provides an interface for external task data crawlers", because it will ease integration between Monocle and the
various task trackers available in the market.

A Monocle operator will need to write the crawler for its
own task tracker. However, over the time, operators might have written crawlers for most popular systems and released them under a open source license.

From the Monocle side, we provide a clear API for a task tracker
crawler to push task related data to Monocle. Each task data sent to Monocle must at least set a predifined set of generic attributes like
"severity", "change_url", "title", ... The monocle API is then able to
find corresponding Changes in the database that match the "change_url" field.

Each changes get a new attribute called "task_data" that is a list of
related task data records. Indeed multiple tasks might be related to a
single change.

Also, Monocle keeps track of task data that do not match any Changes in the
database. The Monocle change crawlers engine triggers a search for adoption of orphaned task data.
cot_answer:
To select the best option, let's evaluate each option based on the decision drivers provided:

1. **Simple implementation**: 
   - **Monocle API provides an interface for external task data crawlers**: This option suggests that Monocle provides an API that allows external crawlers to interface with it. This could potentially simplify the implementation because it leverages existing external crawlers, assuming they are already available and compatible.
   - **Monocle provides crawlers for most popular task trackers**: This option implies that Monocle itself would provide the crawlers. This could be simpler for the end-user since they wouldn't need to set up or manage external crawlers, but it might be more complex for Monocle to implement and maintain these crawlers.

2. **No assumption about the tasks tracker**:
   - **Monocle API provides an interface for external task data crawlers**: This option aligns well with the requirement of making no assumptions about the task tracker, as it allows for flexibility in using any external crawler that can interface with the API.
   - **Monocle provides crawlers for most popular task trackers**: This option might make some assumptions about the task trackers, as it would need to specifically support the most popular ones. This could limit flexibility if a user is using a less common task tracker.

3. **Support of a set of generic fields related to a task**:
   - **Monocle API provides an interface for external task data crawlers**: This option could support generic fields if the API is designed to be flexible and accommodate various data structures from different crawlers.
   - **Monocle provides crawlers for most popular task trackers**: This option might also support generic fields, but it would depend on how the crawlers are implemented and whether they can handle different data structures.

Considering these points, the option "Monocle API provides an interface for external task data crawlers" seems to be the better choice. It offers a simpler implementation by leveraging existing external crawlers, makes no assumptions about the task tracker, and can potentially support a set of generic fields if the API is designed flexibly. 

Therefore, the best option is: **Monocle API provides an interface for external task data crawlers**.
comparison_result: 213 - Yes // Both decisions conclude that providing an API for external task data crawlers is the best option.

## Context and Problem Statement

How do we merge contributor identities across code review systems ?

## Decision Drivers

* Do not complexify the EL query system
* Identities can be configured via the Monocle configuration file

## Considered Options

* [option 1] Identities are described by the Monocle operator into the configuration file.
  Queries result is amended to group/merge returned objects based on identities definitions.
  EL Query builder must check identities definitions and adds OR clause on all fields related
  to authorship like authors/committers/.... 
* [option 2] Identities are described by the Monocle operator into the configuration file.
  The operator runs a tool to update the EL database object to update authorship fields.
  No change needed on the query system.
human_decision:
# 8. Unify idents across code review systems

* Status: accepted
* Deciders: Fabien Boucher
* Date: 2021-03-11

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "[option 2]", Simpler implementation, better query performance (no complexification of queries) and no potential metrics errorneous results returned compared
to "[option 1]".

Here is a configuration example.

```
idents:
  - ident: John Doe
    aliases:
      - github.com/john-doe
      - review.opendev.org/John Doe/12345
```


### Negative Consequences

* A tool need to crawl the whole index to discover objects to update. However this
  operation should not happen often.
cot_answer:
To select the best option for merging contributor identities across code review systems, let's evaluate the two options based on the decision drivers provided:

### Decision Drivers:
1. **Do not complexify the EL query system**: This means that any solution that adds complexity to the query system should be avoided.
2. **Identities can be configured via the Monocle configuration file**: This suggests that the configuration file is a preferred method for managing identities.

### Considered Options:

#### Option 1:
- **Description**: Identities are described by the Monocle operator in the configuration file. The query results are amended to group/merge returned objects based on identity definitions. The EL Query builder must check identity definitions and add OR clauses on all fields related to authorship like authors/committers.
- **Impact on EL Query System**: This option requires changes to the query system, as it involves adding logic to check identity definitions and modify queries accordingly. This could potentially complexify the query system.
- **Configuration**: Identities are managed via the Monocle configuration file, which aligns with the decision driver.

#### Option 2:
- **Description**: Identities are described by the Monocle operator in the configuration file. The operator runs a tool to update the EL database object to update authorship fields. No change is needed on the query system.
- **Impact on EL Query System**: This option does not require any changes to the query system, as the identity merging is handled outside of the query process. This aligns with the decision driver to avoid complexifying the query system.
- **Configuration**: Identities are managed via the Monocle configuration file, which aligns with the decision driver.

### Evaluation:
- **Complexity of EL Query System**: Option 2 is preferable because it does not introduce additional complexity to the query system.
- **Configuration via Monocle**: Both options satisfy this requirement.

### Conclusion:
Given the decision drivers, Option 2 is the best choice. It allows for identity management via the Monocle configuration file without adding complexity to the EL query system. The identity merging is handled by a separate tool, ensuring that the query system remains simple and efficient.
comparison_result: 214 - Yes // Both decisions align in choosing Option 2 for its simplicity and efficiency in managing identities without complexifying the query system.

* good integration with reverse proxy servers like Nginx and Apache.
* support Flask in a simple and performant way

* Date: 2020-05-09

industry. It is not the most performant but it has good performances

   - **Production-ready**: Meinheld is also a production-ready server, but it is less commonly used compared to uWSGI.
   - **Integration with reverse proxies**: Meinheld can be used with reverse proxies like Nginx, but it is not as commonly paired with them as uWSGI.
   - **Support for Flask**: Meinheld is designed to work with WSGI applications, including Flask. It is known for its performance, especially for applications with long-lived connections.

### Evaluation:
- **uWSGI** is a more established and widely used option in production environments. It has a strong track record of integration with Nginx and Apache, making it a reliable choice for serving Flask applications.
- **Meinheld** is a performant server, particularly for specific use cases like long-lived connections, but it is not as commonly used or as well-documented as uWSGI in the context of integration with reverse proxies.

### Conclusion:
Based on the decision drivers and the evaluation of the options, **uWSGI** is the best choice for serving the API using a production-ready server. It offers excellent integration with reverse proxies and robust support for Flask applications, making it a reliable and performant option.

## Context and Problem Statement

> Dex requires persisting state to perform various tasks such as track refresh tokens, preventing replays, and rotating keys.

What persistence option should we use?

## Decision Drivers

* CRDs add complexity
* Storage adds complexity

## Considered Options

* Use ["memory" storage](https://github.com/dexidp/helm-charts/tree/master/charts/dex#minimal-configuration)
* Use [CRD-based storage](https://dexidp.io/docs/storage/#kubernetes-custom-resource-definitions-crds)
human_decision:
# [Superseded by [ADR-0017](0017-persist-dex.md)] Do not persist Dex

* Status: superseded by [ADR-0017](0017-persist-dex.md)
* Deciders: Compliant Kubernetes Architecture Meeting
* Date: 2021-04-29

Technical Story: [Reduce Helmfile concurrency for improved predictability](https://github.com/elastisys/compliantkubernetes-apps/issues/402#issuecomment-827476433)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "use memory", because it simplified operations with little negative impact.

### Positive Consequences

* Dex brings no additional CRDs, which simplified upgrades.
* Dex brings no state, which simplified upgrades.

### Negative Consequences

* The authentication flow is disrupted, if Dex is rebooted *exactly* during an authentication flow. There is no user impact if Dex is restarted after the [JWT](https://jwt.io/) was issued. Cristian tested this with `kubectl` and Grafana. Since we will only reboot Dex during maintenance windows, this is unlikely to be an issue in the foreseeable future.

## Other Considerations

If Dex becomes a bottleneck and needs replication, or if we want to avoid disrupting authentication flows during operations on Dex, we will have to revisit this ADR.
cot_answer:
To determine the best persistence option for Dex, let's evaluate the two considered options based on the decision drivers provided.

### Decision Drivers Analysis

1. **CRDs add complexity**: 
   - CRD-based storage involves using Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions, which can introduce additional complexity in terms of setup, management, and maintenance. This complexity arises from the need to define and manage custom resources within the Kubernetes cluster.

2. **Storage adds complexity**: 
   - Any form of persistent storage, whether it's a database or a file system, adds complexity due to the need for configuration, scaling, backup, and recovery processes. This is true for both CRD-based storage and other forms of persistent storage.

### Considered Options

1. **Use "memory" storage**:
   - **Pros**: 
     - Simplicity: Memory storage is straightforward to set up and does not require any additional infrastructure or configuration.
     - No external dependencies: It does not rely on external systems or resources, reducing the overall complexity.
   - **Cons**: 
     - Volatility: Memory storage is ephemeral and will lose all data upon restart, which may not be suitable for production environments where persistence is required.

2. **Use CRD-based storage**:
   - **Pros**: 
     - Persistence: Data is stored in the Kubernetes cluster, providing persistence across restarts.
     - Integration: Leverages Kubernetes-native resources, which can be beneficial if the environment is already heavily using Kubernetes.
   - **Cons**: 
     - Complexity: As noted, CRDs add complexity in terms of setup and management.
     - Kubernetes dependency: Ties the solution to a Kubernetes environment, which may not be ideal if portability is a concern.

### Conclusion

Given the decision drivers that emphasize minimizing complexity, the "memory" storage option is the simplest and least complex choice. However, it is important to consider the trade-off of losing data persistence across restarts. If the environment is non-production or if the persistence of state is not critical, "memory" storage is the best option.

If persistence is crucial and the environment is already Kubernetes-centric, and the team is comfortable managing CRDs, then CRD-based storage could be considered despite its complexity.

**Final Recommendation**: Use "memory" storage if minimizing complexity is the primary concern and data persistence across restarts is not critical.
comparison_result: 216 - Yes // Both decisions align on using "memory" storage due to its simplicity and minimal complexity.

## Context and Problem Statement

Compliant Kubernetes promises: "Multi-cloud. Open source. Compliant". So far, we delivered on our multi-cloud promise by using our in-house `ck8s-cluster` implementation. This strategy feels unsustainable for two reasons: First, we don't have the resources to catch up and keep up with open source projects in the cluster life-cycle space. Second, we don't want to differentiate on how to set up vanilla Kubernetes cluster, i.e., lower in the Kubernetes stack. Rather we want to differentiate on services on top of vanilla Kubernetes clusters.

## Decision Drivers

* We want to differentiate on top of vanilla Kubernetes cluster.
* We want to be able to run Compliant Kubernetes on top of as many cloud providers as possible.
* We promise building on top of best-of-breeds open source projets.
* We want to reduce burden with developing and maintaining our in-house tooling for cluster life-cycle management.

## Considered Options

* [Rancher](https://rancher.com/)
* [kubeadm via in-house tools (ck8s-cluster)](https://github.com/elastisys/ck8s-cluster)
* [kubespray](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kubespray)
* [kops](https://github.com/kubernetes/kops)
human_decision:
# Use Kubespray for Cluster Life-cycle

* Status: accepted
* Deciders: Lars, Johan, Cristian, Emil, Viktor, Geoff, Ewnetu, Fredrik (potentially others who attended the architecture meeting, but I can't remember)
* Date: 2020-11-17

## Decision Outcome

We chose kubespray, because it is best aligned with our interests, both feature- and roadmap-wise. It has a large community and is expected to be well maintained in the future. It uses kubeadm for domain knowledge on how to set up Kubernetes clusters.

### Positive Consequences

* We learn how to use a widely-used tool for cluster lifecycle management.
* We support many cloud providers.
* We can differentiate on top of vanilla Kubernetes.

### Negative Consequences

* We need training on kubespray.
* We need to port our tooling and practices to kubespray.
* We need to port `compliantkubernetes-apps` to work on kubespray.

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Rancher

* Good, because it provides cluster life-cycle management at scale.
* Bad, because it creates clusters in an opinionated way, which is insufficiently flexible for our needs.
* Bad, because it is not a community project, hence entails long-term licensing uncertainty.

### kubeadm via in-house tool (ck8s-cluster)

* Good, because we know it and we built it.
* Good, because it works well for current use-cases.
* Bad, because it entails a lot of effort to develop and maintain.
* Bad, because it is lagging behind feature-wise with other cluster life-cycle solutions.

### kops

* Good, because it integrates well with the underlying cloud provider (e.g., AWS).
* Bad, because it supports fewer cloud providers than kubespray.

NOTE: In the future, we might want to support `compliantkubernetes-apps` on top of both kops and kubespray, but this does not seem to bring value just now.
cot_answer:
To select the best option for managing Kubernetes clusters, let's evaluate each of the considered options against the decision drivers outlined in the context and problem statement.

### Decision Drivers:
1. **Differentiate on top of vanilla Kubernetes cluster**: The focus is on building services on top of Kubernetes rather than managing the cluster itself.
2. **Run on as many cloud providers as possible**: The solution should be flexible and support multiple cloud environments.
3. **Build on best-of-breed open source projects**: Preference for widely adopted and well-supported open source solutions.
4. **Reduce burden of developing and maintaining in-house tooling**: Minimize the need for custom development and maintenance.

### Considered Options:

1. **Rancher**:
   - **Differentiation**: Rancher provides a comprehensive platform for managing Kubernetes clusters, which might limit the ability to differentiate on top of vanilla Kubernetes.
   - **Multi-cloud Support**: Rancher supports multiple cloud providers and on-premise environments.
   - **Open Source**: Rancher is an open-source project with a strong community and enterprise support.
   - **Maintenance Burden**: Using Rancher reduces the need for in-house development and maintenance of cluster management tools.

2. **kubeadm via in-house tools (ck8s-cluster)**:
   - **Differentiation**: Using kubeadm allows for a vanilla Kubernetes setup, but maintaining in-house tools for lifecycle management is against the goal of reducing maintenance burden.
   - **Multi-cloud Support**: kubeadm can be used on various cloud providers, but the in-house tool may limit flexibility.
   - **Open Source**: kubeadm is a widely used open-source tool, but the in-house tool may not be as robust or widely supported.
   - **Maintenance Burden**: High, due to the need to maintain in-house tools.

3. **kubespray**:
   - **Differentiation**: Kubespray provides a way to set up vanilla Kubernetes clusters, allowing differentiation on top.
   - **Multi-cloud Support**: Supports multiple cloud providers and on-premise environments.
   - **Open Source**: Kubespray is a well-regarded open-source project with a strong community.
   - **Maintenance Burden**: Lower than in-house tools, as it leverages a community-supported project.

4. **kops**:
   - **Differentiation**: Primarily used for AWS, which may limit differentiation if other cloud providers are needed.
   - **Multi-cloud Support**: Primarily focused on AWS, with some support for other environments.
   - **Open Source**: Kops is an open-source project with a strong community, but its focus is more on AWS.
   - **Maintenance Burden**: Lower than in-house tools, but may require additional work for non-AWS environments.

### Conclusion:
Based on the decision drivers, **Kubespray** appears to be the best option. It allows for differentiation on top of vanilla Kubernetes, supports multiple cloud providers, is a well-supported open-source project, and reduces the maintenance burden compared to in-house tools. Rancher is also a strong contender, but it may limit differentiation due to its comprehensive platform approach.
comparison_result: 217 - Yes // Both decisions conclude that Kubespray is the best option for managing Kubernetes clusters.

## Context and Problem Statement

> Dex requires persisting state to perform various tasks such as track refresh tokens, preventing replays, and rotating keys.

What persistence option should we use?

## Decision Drivers

* CRDs add complexity
* Storage adds complexity
* We want to frequently reboot Nodes for security patching
* We want to deliver excellent user experience

## Considered Options

* Use ["memory" storage](https://github.com/dexidp/helm-charts/tree/master/charts/dex#minimal-configuration)
* Use [CRD-based storage](https://dexidp.io/docs/storage/#kubernetes-custom-resource-definitions-crds)
human_decision:
# Persist Dex

* Status: accepted
* Deciders: Compliant Kubernetes Architecture Meeting
* Date: 2021-11-16

Technical Story: [Enable Dex persistence](https://github.com/elastisys/compliantkubernetes-apps/issues/680)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "use CRD-based storage", because it improves user experience when Nodes are rebooted.

As required for "API-changing" Compliant Kubernetes layers, Dex needs to be installed from a separate Helmfile, e.g., `05-dex.yaml`.

With "memory" storage, Dex loses the OpenID keys when restarted, which leads to the user being forced to eventually re-login. Worst off, this forced re-login happens unexpectedly from the user's perspective, when the Kubernetes apiserver chooses to refresh the OpenID keys.

Here is the experiment to illustrate the issue:

```console
$ curl https://dex.$DOMAIN/.well-known/openid-configuration > before-openid-configuration.json
$ curl https://dex.$DOMAIN/keys > before-keys.json

$ kubectl delete pods -n dex -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=dex

$ curl https://dex.$DOMAIN/.well-known/openid-configuration > after-openid-configuration.json
$ curl https://dex.$DOMAIN/keys > after-keys.json

$ diff -y before-openid-configuration.json after-openid-configuration.json
[empty output, no differences]

$ diff -y before-keys.json after-keys.json
[all keys are replaced]
```

### Positive Consequences

* Nodes which host Dex can be rebooted for security patching
* User experience is optimized

### Negative Consequences

* Dex will have a more permissions in the Service Cluster (see [`rbac.yaml`](https://github.com/dexidp/helm-charts/blob/dex-0.6.3/charts/dex/templates/rbac.yaml))
* We will need to closely monitor migration steps for Dex
cot_answer:
To determine the best persistence option for Dex, let's evaluate the two considered options against the decision drivers:

1. **Use "memory" storage:**
   - **Complexity:** Memory storage is generally simpler to implement as it doesn't require additional infrastructure or configuration. It avoids the complexity associated with CRDs and external storage systems.
   - **Node Reboots:** Memory storage is volatile, meaning all data is lost when the application or node is restarted. This is a significant drawback given the requirement to frequently reboot nodes for security patching, as it would lead to loss of state and potentially disrupt user experience.
   - **User Experience:** Due to the volatility of memory storage, user experience could be negatively impacted by frequent reboots, as users might need to re-authenticate or lose session data.

2. **Use CRD-based storage:**
   - **Complexity:** CRD-based storage adds complexity due to the need to manage Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions. However, it provides a more robust and persistent storage solution compared to memory storage.
   - **Node Reboots:** CRD-based storage is persistent across node reboots, as the data is stored in the Kubernetes cluster. This aligns well with the requirement to frequently reboot nodes without losing state.
   - **User Experience:** By maintaining state across reboots, CRD-based storage can provide a more consistent and reliable user experience, as users won't be affected by node reboots.

**Conclusion:**
Given the decision drivers, particularly the need to frequently reboot nodes and deliver an excellent user experience, CRD-based storage is the better option. While it introduces some complexity, it ensures persistence and reliability, which are crucial for maintaining state and providing a seamless user experience. Therefore, the recommended persistence option for Dex is to use CRD-based storage.
comparison_result: 218 - Yes // Both decisions conclude that CRD-based storage is the better option for Dex persistence.

## Context and Problem Statement

There are three  major decisions we need to make that have an impact on what technologies are used and how the code is implemented:
- Should this be a single process or multiple processes?
- Should distinct pieces of functionality live in separate GitHub repos?
- How many threads should be used?

## Decision Drivers

* I want to use RocksDB in any solution, but RocksDB does not support multiple processes unless all of them are readonly. Since I need a writer, I am forced into having all reads/writes happening on a single process.
* Multiple repos ended up being a distributed monolith, and I needed a `wx-shared` repo to hold shared functionality and domain structs. I do not want to deal with this again.
* ZeroMQ was fun to learn, but the serde and IPC added a layer of complication whenever I tried refactoring or troubleshooting.

## Considered Options

* Old way: multi-repo, multi-process
* Single-repo, multi-process
    - This could be mono-crate or use multiple crates in a workspace
* Single-repo, single process
human_decision:
# sware's general architecture should be a single process, multi-threaded mono-repo

* Status: accepted
* Date: 2020-04-14

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: `Single-repo, single process` because it keeps things simple and allows me to focus on writing new features and making the existing feature more bulletproof instead of trying to wire up multiple repositories/processes.

### Positive Consequences

* Reduced complexity is easier to read and understand
* Reducing the repos involved allows the shared library to just be a module that all other code uses
* Removing multiple processes from the solution means that IPC isn't needed, which means all of the code around ZMQ transport and serde can be removed. This greatly simplifies interactions with the store.

### Negative Consequences

* Unable to scale horizontally if needed, however RocksDB makes that difficult to do anyways
* I don't get to learn with functionality like crate workspaces, ZMQ, or MPSC queues
* Have to rebuild RocksDB when making changes to unrelated things like API routes
cot_answer:
To select the best option, let's evaluate each of the considered options against the decision drivers and the context provided.

### Decision Drivers Analysis

1. **RocksDB Requirement**: 
   - RocksDB does not support multiple processes unless they are all readonly. Since a writer is needed, this necessitates all reads/writes happening in a single process.

2. **Repository Structure**:
   - The previous experience with multiple repos led to a distributed monolith, requiring a shared repo for common functionality. This was undesirable, indicating a preference for a single repository to avoid complexity and maintenance issues.

3. **Complexity with ZeroMQ**:
   - ZeroMQ added complexity due to serialization/deserialization (serde) and inter-process communication (IPC), which complicated refactoring and troubleshooting. This suggests a preference for reducing inter-process communication complexity.

### Considered Options Evaluation

1. **Old way: multi-repo, multi-process**
   - **Pros**: Potentially allows for separation of concerns and modularity.
   - **Cons**: Conflicts with the RocksDB requirement (single process for writes), leads to a distributed monolith, and increases complexity with ZeroMQ. This option does not align well with the decision drivers.

2. **Single-repo, multi-process**
   - **Pros**: Keeps all code in one place, potentially reducing the distributed monolith issue.
   - **Cons**: Still conflicts with the RocksDB requirement (single process for writes) and retains complexity with ZeroMQ for inter-process communication. This option partially addresses the repository issue but not the process or complexity issues.

3. **Single-repo, single process**
   - **Pros**: Fully aligns with the RocksDB requirement by ensuring all reads/writes happen in a single process. Avoids the distributed monolith issue by keeping everything in one repository. Eliminates the complexity associated with ZeroMQ and inter-process communication.
   - **Cons**: May require careful design to manage concurrency and scalability within a single process.

### Conclusion

Given the decision drivers and the analysis of each option, the **Single-repo, single process** option is the best choice. It aligns with the need to use RocksDB effectively, avoids the pitfalls of a distributed monolith, and reduces complexity by eliminating inter-process communication. This option provides a simpler, more maintainable solution that meets the requirements and addresses past challenges.
comparison_result: 219 - Yes // Both decisions conclude that the single-repo, single-process option is the best choice due to simplicity and alignment with RocksDB requirements.

## Context and Problem Statement

A repository for each microservice or only one for all of them?

## Decision Drivers

* Development agility
* Microservices decoupling
* Big-picture scenario visibility

## Considered Options

* A repository for each microservice, and another for service definitions
* A single repository with decoupled microservices including service definitions
human_decision:
# Have a single repository for all microservices

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: A single repository for all microservices and service definitions this time, because this way its easy to get a big picture of the approach, for the purposes of this example.

In production, I'll consider separating microservices and service definitions on repos, in order to have separate triggers on CI for them.

I think [this approach](https://medium.com/namely-labs/how-we-build-grpc-services-at-namely-52a3ae9e7c35) will be a good fit for address this concern in production.
cot_answer:
To determine the best option for managing repositories in a microservices architecture, let's evaluate the decision drivers and the considered options step by step.

### Decision Drivers

1. **Development Agility**: This refers to the ability of the development team to quickly and efficiently make changes, deploy updates, and manage the codebase. A setup that allows for independent development and deployment of microservices can enhance agility.

2. **Microservices Decoupling**: This involves ensuring that each microservice is independent and can be developed, deployed, and scaled without affecting others. Decoupling is a core principle of microservices architecture.

3. **Big-picture Scenario Visibility**: This is about maintaining an overview of the entire system, understanding how different services interact, and ensuring coherence across the architecture.

### Considered Options

1. **A repository for each microservice, and another for service definitions**:
   - **Pros**:
     - **Development Agility**: Each microservice can be developed and deployed independently, allowing teams to work in parallel without interference.
     - **Microservices Decoupling**: This option naturally enforces decoupling, as each service is in its own repository.
   - **Cons**:
     - **Big-picture Scenario Visibility**: It might be challenging to maintain an overview of the entire system since the code is spread across multiple repositories.

2. **A single repository with decoupled microservices including service definitions**:
   - **Pros**:
     - **Big-picture Scenario Visibility**: Having all code in a single repository can make it easier to see the entire system and understand interactions between services.

* Status: proposed
* Deciders: Leon Kiefer
* Date: 2019-12-13

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Send SHA256 hash of Base64Url encoded json", because this method is platform independent and not much session state is required.

### Positive Consequences <!-- optional -->

* The JWT really function as a verification token for the other requests.
* Can be applied to all json data that must be verified.

### Negative Consequences <!-- optional -->

* The json must be transferred in Base64Url encoding

## Pros and Cons of the Options <!-- optional -->

### Transfer complete json via secure channel

The complete json data is transferred using a secure channel, like a JWT Token Claim.
The secure channel takes care of the Integrity and the transport.

* Good, because well known solutions can be used.
* Good, because very secure.
* Bad, because depending on selected secure channel many data have to be stored in a session state.
* Bad, because there are limitations how many data can be transferred at once using a secure channel.

### Send SHA256 hash of Base64Url encoded json

The json is encoded with Base64Url encoding (RFC 4648).
The Base64 String is then transferred instead of the raw json.
For the Base64 string the message digest using SHA256 (FIPS PUB 180-4) is computed and used to verify the integrity.
The message digest is a sequence of bytes and should be encoded to a lower-case hex string to transfer it over a secure channel like JWT.

* Good, because the Integrity of the json can be verified simply.
* Good, because only the small hex encoded message digest must be transferred over a secure channel.
* Bad, because the json is transferred Base64 encoded and must be decoded before use.
* Bad, because this must be implemented by hand.

### Send SHA256 hash of formatted json

The json can be transferred in any format.
To verify the integrity, the json is formatted in a way, that the same json info set result in the same json string representation on all platforms.
This json string is then hashed using SHA256 (FIPS PUB 180-4) and the message digest can be used the verify the integrity.
The message digest is a sequence of bytes and can be Base64Url encoded to transferred it over a secure channel like JWT.

* Good, because only the small Base64 encoded message digest must be transferred over a secure channel.
* Good, because json can be be transferred as is.
* Bad, because difficult to get a consistent formatting across platforms.
* Bad, because heavily depends on the json formatting library
* Bad, because this must be implemented by hand.

External services must authorize web clients to the WebSocket API.
The WebSocket API is stateless and not maintain a user Session with Cookies.
Only little data should be stored for an open WebSocket connection.

* JWT from pre-shared keys

# Use JSON Web Tokens

* Status: accepted
* Deciders: Leon Kiefer, Per Pascal Seeland, Anett Seeland
* Date: 2019-11-07

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "JWT from pre-shared keys", because the WebSocket API is loosely coupled and it is well supported on many platforms.

### Positive Consequences

* Simple to implement
* Authorization data can be send in a portable and verifiable way

### Negative Consequences

* The shared keys must be handled

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### JWT from pre-shared keys

External service and WebSocket API have a pre-shared key (this does not mean it's a symmetric key).
Each external service has it's own pre-shared key to identify it.
The external services uses the pre-shared key to generate JWTs and add authorization data in the JWT Claims to allow clients access to parts of the WebSocket API.

* Good, because it is simple to implement
* Good, because many libraries available for almost all platforms
* Good, because authorization data can be included in the JWT
* Bad, because the pre-shared keys must be handled by the services

### Basic Auth

The client uses credentials like username and password to authenticate to the WebSocket API.
The WebSocket API manages the access control for clients and the external service can give clients the access.

* Good, because authorization is done only on the server side
* Bad, because user management must be implemented in the WebSocket API
* Bad, because access control must be implemented in the WebSocket API
* Bad, because each client need own credentials

### OAuth 2.0

Similar to [Basic Auth](#basic-auth) but the authorization is done using OAuth 2.0.

* Good, because integration of OAuth 2.0 Service
* Bad, because an OAuth 2.0 is required and must be configured for the correct access control
* Bad, because user management must be implemented in OAuth 2.0 Service

When using JSON Web Tokens generating signatures and verifying them is an important task.
JWTs can be signed using a secret (with the HMAC algorithm) or a public/private key pair using RSA or ECDSA.
When implementing JWTs one must decide which method to use.

## Decision Drivers

* Multi tenant support with own keys for each tenant

## Considered Options

* Asymmetric JWT signing
* Symmetric JWT signing

* Status: accepted
* Deciders: Leon Kiefer, Per Pascal Seeland
* Date: 2020-05-11

Technical Story: https://github.com/VirtualProgrammingLab/viplab-websocket-api/issues/11

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Asymmetric JWT signing", because it the only option which allow to use different keys for different tenants.

### Positive Consequences

* multiple keys are supported

### Negative Consequences

* complex management of keys

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Asymmetric JWT signing

A RSA or ECDSA key pair is used for signing and verification.
The JWTs signed by the external services using their own private key.
Each private/public key pair has a key id and the public key is added as known key to the websocket-api.
The websocket-api uses the key id of the JWT to find the corresponding known public and use it to validate the JWT Token signature.

* Good, because multiple tenants can use the same websocket-api service with different keys
* Good, because adding or revoking of single tenant key is possible
* Bad, because setup of the private and public keys is complicated
* Bad, because multiple keys must be managed

### Symmetric JWT signing

The HMAC algorithm with a shared secret is used for signing and verification.
All the external services must know the shared secret of the websocket-api to generate valid JWTs.
The websocket-api use it secret to validate all JWTs.

* Good, because implementation very simple
* Good, because only a simple secret (string) must be managed
* Bad, because all tenants use the same shared secret
* Bad, because changing the secret require changes to all tenants

## Links

* [ADR-0001](0001-use-json-web-tokens.md)

- **JWTs**: JSON Web Tokens are used for securely transmitting information between parties as a JSON object. They are commonly used for authentication and information exchange.
- **Signature Generation and Verification**: Ensures the integrity and authenticity of the token.
- **Signing Methods**: 
  - **Symmetric (HMAC)**: Uses a single secret key for both signing and verification.
  - **Asymmetric (RSA/ECDSA)**: Uses a pair of keys, a private key for signing and a public key for verification.

### Decision Drivers
- **Multi-tenant Support with Own Keys for Each Tenant**: This implies that each tenant should have its own unique key or key pair for signing JWTs. This is crucial for isolating tenants and ensuring that one tenant's tokens cannot be verified or tampered with by another tenant.
